content: The Nurses' Health Study, initiated in 1976 by Dr. Frank Speizer, and its successor, the Nurses' Health Study II, launched in 1989 by Dr. Walter Willett, are among the most comprehensive and long-term epidemiological studies focused on the health of older women. These studies have tracked 121,700 female registered nurses since the mid-1970s to investigate risk factors for cancer and cardiovascular disease. They represent some of the largest investigations into chronic disease risk factors in women ever conducted. The studies involve collaboration among clinicians, epidemiologists, and statisticians at the Channing Laboratory, with participation from institutions such as Harvard Medical School, Harvard School of Public Health, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston Children’s Hospital, and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. In 1980, dietary assessments, aspirin use, and colon examination data were incorporated into the original study. The study design initially surveyed nurses aged 30 to 55 in 1976, with follow-up surveys conducted every two years. Over time, additional questions were added, including a dietary assessment in 1980. Deaths reported by next of kin or postal authorities were followed up, and in cases suggestive of cardiovascular disease or coronary heart disease, further documentation, such as autopsy reports, was obtained when possible. The mortality follow-up rate exceeds 98%. To date, the studies have resulted in the publication of over 100 peer-reviewed papers. Specific investigations have examined topics such as the effects of low-dose aspirin and vitamin E on cardiovascular disease and cancer prevention, the impact of low-fat diets on health, and the relationship between various lifestyle factors and chronic diseases. These findings have significantly advanced our understanding of women's health and have informed public health recommendations.
